review_notes: I read the whole file and checked the main definitions against Mathlib. `permutationLinear` is the same map as `LinearMap.funLeft ℂ ℂ π`, so I reported it. I did not report `matchingSetoid` (it already uses `Relation.EqvGen.setoid`) or `matchingEquiv` (I found no Mathlib equivalent for the quotient-lifting equivalence). `permutationDistance` is a rank-of-difference metric, and I found no Mathlib counterpart. I did not search the rest of the repo for other uses of `permutationLinear`. A grep count showed 9 occurrences, all in this file, so replacing it affects only this file. I could not compile any replacement, so the `simp` lemma behaviour after the change is untested.

findings.excerpt:
def permutationLinear {ι : Type*} (π : Equiv.Perm ι) : (ι → ℂ) →ₗ[ℂ] (ι → ℂ) where
  toFun f := f ∘ π
findings.problem: `permutationLinear π` is precomposition with `π` as a ℂ-linear map on `ι → ℂ`. That is `LinearMap.funLeft ℂ ℂ π`, which Mathlib already defines for any function `m → n` with `toFun := (· ∘ f)`. The new definition has the same `toFun` and the same `rfl` proofs of additivity and homogeneity. It adds no new meaning, and it has no `funLeft_apply`, `funLeft_comp` or `funLeft_id` lemmas. Every use here is `permutationLinear π`, which appears only in this file (9 occurrences).
findings.proposed_change: Remove the def and use `LinearMap.funLeft ℂ ℂ π` directly. If the name is worth keeping, make it an abbreviation: `abbrev permutationLinear (π : Equiv.Perm ι) : (ι → ℂ) →ₗ[ℂ] (ι → ℂ) := LinearMap.funLeft ℂ ℂ π`. Either way the existing `simp [permutationLinear, ...]` call in `permutationDistance_eq_zero` can use `LinearMap.funLeft_apply`.
findings.benefit: The file reuses Mathlib's `funLeft` API instead of keeping a second, identical linear map. Later results about composition and surjectivity or injectivity of `funLeft` apply to it without conversion.

evidence.excerpt:
def funLeft (f : m → n) : (n → M) →ₗ[R] m → M where
  toFun := (· ∘ f)
theorem funLeft_apply (f : m → n) (g : n → M) (i : m) : funLeft R M f g i = g (f i)
